title: Read-Write Locks and Lock Granularity
objectives: Decide when a read-write lock beats a plain mutex
Raise a lock’s throughput ceiling by shortening or splitting critical sections
Avoid writer starvation and upgrade deadlocks

cards.title: Many readers or one writer
cards.body: A read-write lock lets any number of threads hold it for reading at once, or exactly one thread hold it for writing. It helps when reads are frequent, writes are rare and the read section is long enough to matter. Every reader still updates a shared count when it enters and leaves, so for very short sections the lock’s own bookkeeping can cost more than the work it protects.

cards.title: Worked example: one lock caps the whole service
cards.body: A cache protected by a single mutex.
steps: Each lookup holds the lock for 2 µs (illustrative)
Only one thread can be inside at a time, so the cache serves at most 1 ÷ 2 µs = 500,000 lookups a second, however many cores there are
Split the cache into 16 shards by key hash, each with its own lock
With keys spread evenly and enough cores, the ceiling rises toward 16 × 500,000 = 8 million lookups a second
Shortening the section to 1 µs (no allocation or logging inside it) doubles every one of those ceilings

cards.title: Trap: writers that never get in
cards.body: Many read-write locks prefer readers: a new reader may enter while a writer is waiting, as long as another reader holds the lock. Under steady read traffic there is always some reader inside, so the writer waits indefinitely and the data it should update goes stale. Choose a lock that blocks new readers once a writer queues, or keep read sections short enough that gaps appear.

cards.title: Misconception: you can upgrade a read lock in place
cards.body: Two threads each hold the read lock and both decide to write. Each asks for the write lock while still holding its read lock, each waits for the other reader to leave, and neither ever will: a deadlock. Release the read lock, take the write lock, and re-check the condition, since another thread may have changed it in between, or use a lock with an explicit single-upgrader mode.

cards.title: Finer locks bring new rules
cards.body: Splitting one lock into many raises throughput but makes operations that span several shards harder. Moving an item between two shards needs both locks, and taking them in different orders in different threads can deadlock, so always lock shards in a fixed order such as by index. Operations over every shard, like a total count, either lock all of them in order or accept a value that is only approximately consistent.

questions.prompt: A configuration map is read on every request and rewritten once an hour. Each read copies a few fields in about 50 ns. Which lock choice should you test first?

choices.label: A read-write lock, since reads vastly outnumber writes
A plain mutex, or an immutable snapshot swapped on change
A spin lock, since the hourly write must finish fast
No lock, because readers do not modify the map

questions.explanation: With a 50 ns read section, the read-write lock’s shared reader count becomes the bottleneck, so a mutex is often as fast; swapping in a new immutable snapshot removes locking from reads entirely. The read-write lock seems right by ratio but loses on bookkeeping. A spin lock does nothing for readers, and with no lock, readers can see a half-written map during the hourly change.

questions.prompt: A metrics store uses a read-write lock. Under heavy dashboard traffic, the writer that records new data falls minutes behind. What is the most likely cause?

choices.label: The writer has a lower thread priority than readers
Readers hold the lock longer than the writer does
New readers keep entering while the writer waits
The write lock is recursive and blocks itself

questions.explanation: A reader-preferring lock admits new readers whenever another reader is inside, so with constant reads the writer starves. Thread priority does not change lock admission, longer reads only matter because readers overlap without gaps, and a recursive lock does not block its own holder.

questions.prompt: Two threads hold the same read lock. Each then requests the write lock without releasing its read lock. What happens?

choices.label: Both block forever, each waiting for the other to leave
The first to ask gets the write lock, the other waits
Both get the write lock, because they already hold it
The lock converts both reads into one shared write

questions.explanation: A write lock needs every reader gone, and each thread is a reader the other is waiting on, so neither proceeds. Asking first does not help because the other reader is still inside, write locks are never shared, and no lock merges two readers into a writer.

questions.prompt: A shared hash map is protected by one mutex and profiles show threads waiting on it. Which change usually raises throughput the most?

choices.label: Replace the mutex with a read-write lock of the same scope
Add more threads so that more of them reach the lock
Use a fair lock so waiting threads take turns in order
Shard the map by key hash, each shard with its own lock

questions.explanation: Independent locks per shard let operations on different keys run in parallel, multiplying the ceiling. A read-write lock helps only if reads dominate and are long, more threads lengthen the queue, and a fair lock orders waiting threads without letting more of them in at once.

questions.prompt: Every request holds one global lock for 4 µs. What is the most requests per second the service can complete, however many cores it has?
assumptions: The lock is held only during the 4 µs section
Handing the lock over costs nothing
questions.explanation: Sanity check: real handovers between cores add hundreds of nanoseconds, so the practical ceiling is lower; plan to stay well under it, or shorten and split the section.

questions.prompt: A thread holding a read lock discovers it needs to modify the data. Order the safe steps.

items.label: Acquire the write lock
Make the change if it is still needed, then release the write lock
Release the read lock
Re-check the condition that made the write necessary

questions.explanation: Never wait for the write lock while holding the read lock, and re-check after acquiring because another writer may have acted in the gap.

flashcards.front: When does a read-write lock help?
flashcards.back: Many readers, rare writes, and read sections long enough to outweigh the shared reader count.
1 ÷ time the lock is held per operation, regardless of core count.
Two readers both wait for the write lock while holding their read locks.

mechanism.title: How a read-write lock admits threads
steps: The lock keeps a count of active readers, a flag for an active writer, and usually a count of waiting writers, often packed into one word changed with atomic operations.
A reader may enter if no writer holds the lock; depending on the policy it may also have to wait if a writer is queued. Entering increments the reader count, and leaving decrements it.
A writer may enter only when the reader count is zero and no other writer holds the lock. Waiting threads sleep and are woken when the state changes.

Because every reader writes the shared count, readers on many cores still fight over one cache line. For short sections that traffic, not the waiting, sets the cost, which is why sharded counters or copy-on-write snapshots often beat a read-write lock.
Policies differ: reader preference maximises read throughput but can starve writers; writer preference blocks new readers once a writer waits, so writers progress but reads stall briefly.
Granularity is a separate choice: one lock over everything is simple and safe; per-shard or per-object locks raise throughput, at the cost of lock ordering rules for multi-object operations.

useWhen: Use a read-write lock when reads dominate and each read section does real work, such as walking a structure.
Use sharding when operations touch independent keys.
avoidWhen: Avoid read-write locks around tiny read sections; measure against a mutex.
Avoid upgrading a held read lock in place.

rows: Memory for old copies still in use

numbers.title: What sharding buys
assumptions: Lookups hold the lock for 2 µs; the service needs 3 million lookups a second (illustrative)
Keys are spread evenly by hash
steps: One lock: ceiling 1 ÷ 2 µs = 500,000 a second, six times too few.
Shards needed at the ceiling: 3,000,000 ÷ 500,000 = 6.
Running each shard at no more than 50% of its ceiling keeps waits short: 6 ÷ 0.5 = 12 shards.
Round up to 16 shards, a power of two that lets the shard be picked with a bit mask of the hash.
numbers.result: Sixteen shards give a combined ceiling of 8 million lookups a second, leaving the needed 3 million at under 40% of capacity.

india.title: What the manual says about writer starvation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Linux manual page for pthread_rwlockattr_setkind_np describes the reader-preference setting, which is the default in the GNU C library: a reader receives the lock even if a writer is waiting, and as long as there are readers, the writer will be starved. It also notes that the writer-preference setting is ignored by that library, because supporting recursive read locks would make it deadlock, and offers a non-recursive writer-preferring mode instead.

pitfalls.trap: “Reads outnumber writes, so a read-write lock is faster.”
pitfalls.say: “Only if read sections are long; I’d benchmark it against a mutex and a snapshot swap.”

pitfalls.trap: “Add cores to get past the lock.”
pitfalls.say: “A lock caps throughput at 1 ÷ hold time; I’d shorten or shard it.”

takeaways: Read-write locks help long reads with rare writes.
A lock’s ceiling is one divided by its hold time.
Reader-preferring locks can starve writers.
Never upgrade a read lock while holding it; release, lock, re-check.

interactive.title: Will the read-write lock help?
interactive.prompt: A service’s hot path takes a mutex around a 30 ns hash map lookup. Reads are 99% of operations. A teammate proposes switching to a read-write lock.

choices.label: Probably not: the shared reader count costs about as much as the lookup
choices.feedback: Right: every reader still writes one shared line, so short sections gain little or nothing.

choices.label: Yes, roughly a hundred times faster because readers run in parallel
choices.feedback: Readers overlap only after each has updated the shared count, which is the expensive part here.

choices.label: No, read-write locks are only for reads served from disk
choices.feedback: They work for any data; the issue here is the tiny section, not where the data lives.

interactive.reveal: Measure before switching. For tiny read sections, sharding the map or publishing an immutable copy that readers access without a lock usually beats both a mutex and a read-write lock.

seeAlso.why: Mutual exclusion and why shared data needs a lock at all
Lock ordering prevents deadlocks when you split locks
Atomics explain why a shared reader count is costly

title: How Locks Wait: Spinning, Sleeping and Futexes
objectives: Explain why an uncontended lock needs no system call
Choose between spinning and sleeping from how long a lock is held
Recognise lock convoys and spinning on a preempted holder

cards.title: The fast path stays in user space
cards.body: Modern mutexes are built on a futex (fast user-space mutex): an integer in shared memory changed with atomic instructions. Taking a free lock is one compare-and-swap, with no system call. Only when the lock is already held does the waiter ask the kernel to put it to sleep on that address, and only when someone is waiting does the unlocker ask the kernel to wake one. Uncontended locking therefore costs tens of nanoseconds.

cards.title: Spin or sleep?
cards.body: A waiting thread can spin, retrying the atomic operation in a loop, or sleep in the kernel until woken. Sleeping and waking costs a pair of system calls and a context switch, on the order of microseconds, while spinning costs nothing extra if the lock frees within a few hundred nanoseconds. Most library mutexes spin briefly and then sleep, which suits both short and long hold times.

cards.title: Worked example: pick by hold time
cards.body: Rough costs on one machine (illustrative).
steps: Sleep and wake round trip: about 5 µs of CPU and latency
Lock held for 200 ns: spinning waits about 200 ns; sleeping would cost about 25 times more
Lock held for 1 ms: spinning burns 1 ms of a core doing nothing; sleeping costs 5 µs and frees the core for other work
Unknown or variable hold time: spin for roughly the cost of a sleep, then sleep
Rule of thumb: spin only when holders are running on other cores and sections are short

cards.title: Trap: spinning on a holder that is not running
cards.body: If the thread holding a spin lock is preempted, or the machine has more runnable threads than cores, waiters spin for their whole time slice while the holder waits to be scheduled. On a single core, spinning cannot succeed until the spinner gives up the CPU. User-space code should almost never use a pure spin lock; use the platform mutex, which falls back to sleeping.

cards.title: Misconception: a fair lock is the fast choice
cards.body: Handing the lock directly to the longest waiter sounds fair, but that waiter is asleep, so every hand-off pays a wake-up while the lock sits idle; meanwhile a running thread that could have taken it at once has to queue. Under heavy contention this forms a lock convoy: throughput collapses to one wake-up per acquisition. Most default mutexes are unfair for this reason; reduce contention rather than demanding fairness.

questions.prompt: A program takes and releases an uncontended mutex 10 million times a second. How many system calls does locking add?

choices.label: About 20 million: one each to lock and to unlock
About 10 million, one per lock and pair
Usually none: free locks are taken with an atomic
One per second, when the kernel audits held locks

questions.explanation: With no contention, lock and unlock are atomic operations on a word in user space; the kernel is called only to sleep or to wake a waiter. Two calls per pair would be true of older kernel-object locks, which is why futexes were introduced, and the kernel never audits locks periodically.

questions.prompt: Which situation suits a brief spin before sleeping?

choices.label: A lock held for about 100 ns by threads on other cores
A lock held while a database query runs
A lock on a single-core machine with many threads
A lock held while waiting for a user to click

questions.explanation: A 100 ns hold frees the lock long before a sleep and wake round trip could complete, and the holder is running elsewhere. Holding across a query or a click means milliseconds to seconds of wasted spinning, and on one core the holder cannot run while the waiter spins.

questions.prompt: Under load, a service using a strictly fair (first-come, first-served) lock reaches only a fraction of the throughput of the same code with the default lock. Why?

choices.label: Fair locks use a slower atomic instruction internally
Each hand-off waits for a sleeping thread to wake
Fair locks restrict the program to running on one core
The default lock skips locking whenever load is high

questions.explanation: Handing the lock to the oldest waiter means waking a sleeping thread for every acquisition while running threads queue: a convoy. The atomics are the same, other cores keep running other code, and no correct lock skips locking under load.

questions.prompt: A team replaces a mutex with a hand-written spin lock. On a container limited to 2 CPUs with 16 worker threads, latency gets much worse. Why?

choices.label: Spin locks need a lock-free memory allocator underneath
Spinning uses a lot of memory bandwidth on two cores
Spin locks are invalid inside containers by design
Waiters spin while the holder waits for a CPU to run on

questions.explanation: With 16 runnable threads on 2 CPUs, the holder is often not running, so spinners burn quota without any chance of success. The allocator is irrelevant, bandwidth is a minor effect, and containers place no rule on spin locks.

questions.prompt: A lock is contended 10,000 times a second, and each contended acquisition sleeps and is woken at a cost of about 5 µs of CPU. Roughly how many milliseconds of CPU per second does that cost?
assumptions: Uncontended acquisitions cost almost nothing
Every contended acquisition sleeps once
questions.explanation: Sanity check: 50 ms per second is 5% of one core spent on waiting alone; at 200,000 contended acquisitions a second it would be a whole core, a sign to shard or shorten the lock.

questions.prompt: Order what happens when thread B tries to take a mutex that thread A holds, until B owns it.

items.label: A unlocks, sees waiters, and asks the kernel to wake one
B’s atomic attempt fails and it marks the lock as having waiters
B wakes, retries the atomic, and takes the lock
B asks the kernel to sleep on the lock’s address

questions.explanation: Fast path fails, sleep on the address, unlock wakes a waiter, the waiter retries; only the contended case touches the kernel.

flashcards.back: An atomic integer in user space; the kernel is called only to sleep or wake when the lock is contended.
Spin for holds shorter than a sleep and wake round trip (microseconds); otherwise sleep.
Every hand-off waits for a sleeping thread to wake, so throughput drops to one wake-up per acquisition.

mechanism.title: The life of a contended mutex
steps: The mutex is a word with three states, for example 0 free, 1 locked, and 2 locked with waiters. Locking tries to change 0 to 1 with compare-and-swap; success means the lock is taken without entering the kernel.
On failure the thread may spin for a short while, re-reading the word without writing so it does not fight over the cache line, and trying again when it reads 0.

If the lock is still held, the thread sets the word to 2 and calls the kernel’s futex wait on its address, asking to sleep only if the value is still 2. That check closes the race with an unlock happening at the same moment.
The kernel hashes the address to a wait queue and puts the thread to sleep. No kernel object exists for an uncontended lock; queues appear only while someone waits.

Unlocking sets the word to 0. If it was 2, the unlocker calls futex wake for one waiter. The woken thread competes again; a running thread may take the lock first, which is unfair but keeps the lock busy.
Priority-inheritance and robust variants add kernel bookkeeping so a waiting high-priority thread boosts the holder, or so a lock held by a thread that died can be recovered.

useWhen: Use the platform mutex by default: it spins briefly and then sleeps.
Use spinning only in code that runs with preemption controlled, such as kernels or pinned threads.
avoidWhen: Avoid pure spin locks in ordinary user-space programs.
Avoid strictly fair locks on hot paths unless starvation has been observed.

numbers.title: When contention starts to show
assumptions: A lock held for 1 µs per operation at 300,000 operations a second (illustrative)
A contended acquisition costs about 5 µs of sleep and wake (illustrative)
steps: Lock utilisation: 300,000 × 1 µs = 0.3 s per second, so it is busy 30% of the time.
About 30% of arrivals find it held; with spinning first, most of those waits end within about a microsecond.
If they all slept instead: 300,000 × 0.3 × 5 µs = 0.45 CPU-seconds per second spent sleeping and waking.
A brief spin turns most of that into about 1 µs of spinning each: 90,000 × 1 µs = 0.09 CPU-seconds.
numbers.result: At 30% utilisation, spinning briefly before sleeping cuts wait overhead from almost half a core to under a tenth of one in this example.

india.title: What the manual says futexes are for
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The futex(7) manual page explains that futex operation occurs entirely in user space for the non-contended case, and the kernel is involved only to arbitrate the contended case. It notes that, as any sane design will strive for non-contention, futexes are optimised for this situation: in its bare form a futex is an aligned integer touched only by atomic instructions, with system calls used solely to wait and to wake.

pitfalls.trap: “Mutexes are slow because they’re system calls.”
pitfalls.say: “Uncontended mutexes are a single atomic; I’d measure contention before replacing one.”

pitfalls.trap: “A spin lock will be faster than the mutex.”
pitfalls.say: “Only if holders are always running and sections are tiny; the mutex already spins briefly.”

takeaways: Free locks are taken with one atomic, no system call.
Spin for holds shorter than a sleep and wake; otherwise sleep.
Spinning on a preempted holder wastes whole time slices.
Strict fairness causes convoys; reduce contention instead.

interactive.title: Spin lock or mutex here?
interactive.prompt: A worker pool of 32 threads runs on a 4-CPU container. Each task takes a lock for about 2 µs to update shared state. Someone proposes a pure spin lock to avoid system calls.

choices.label: Keep the mutex: with 32 threads on 4 CPUs, holders are often descheduled
choices.feedback: Right: spinners would burn CPU while the holder waits to run.

choices.label: Use the spin lock: 2 µs is far below the cost of sleeping
choices.feedback: Short holds favour spinning only if the holder is actually running on another core.

choices.label: Use a fair lock so every thread gets its turn in order
choices.feedback: Fair hand-offs wake a sleeping thread each time and make throughput worse.

interactive.reveal: Oversubscription is the deciding fact: with eight threads per CPU, a spinning waiter usually spins on a holder that is not running. A standard mutex already spins briefly and then sleeps, so it gets the benefit of spinning without the worst case.

seeAlso.why: The mutual exclusion that futexes implement
Context switches are the cost a sleeping waiter pays
Priority inheritance is built into some futex variants

title: Priority Inversion and Real-Time Scheduling
objectives: Explain how a high-priority thread ends up waiting on a low-priority one
Use priority inheritance or ceilings to bound the wait
Know what nice values and real-time policies actually change

cards.title: Priorities and policies
cards.body: Normal threads share the CPU in proportion to weights set by their nice value: lower nice means a larger share, but every runnable thread still makes progress. Real-time policies (first-in-first-out and round-robin with priorities from 1 to 99) are strict: a runnable real-time thread always runs before any normal thread, and a higher real-time priority always runs before a lower one.

cards.title: Worked example: the inversion
cards.body: Three threads on one core, with a lock shared by High and Low.
steps: Low takes the lock and starts a 1 ms update
High wakes, preempts Low, and blocks on the lock Low holds
Medium, which needs no lock, wakes and preempts Low because it outranks Low
Medium computes for 50 ms; Low cannot run to release the lock, so High waits 50 ms or more instead of about 1 ms
With priority inheritance, Low runs at High’s priority while High waits, Medium cannot preempt it, and High waits about 1 ms

cards.title: Two ways to bound the wait
cards.body: Priority inheritance raises a lock holder’s priority to that of the highest thread waiting for the lock, for as long as it holds it. A priority ceiling raises any holder to a fixed priority assigned to the lock, so nothing that could contend with it can preempt it. Both keep the inversion to the length of one critical section; both must be enabled on the lock, since ordinary mutexes do neither by default.

cards.title: Trap: a real-time thread that never yields
cards.body: A thread switched to a real-time policy that loops without blocking will starve every normal thread on its core, including the shell you would use to stop it. Linux keeps a safety margin by default, limiting real-time threads to 95% of each second, but a misbehaving real-time thread still slows everything else to a crawl. Give real-time threads only short, bounded work and block between items.

cards.title: Misconception: lower nice fixes latency
cards.body: Nice values change long-run CPU shares between busy threads, not how quickly a thread is woken. A thread waiting on a lock, a disk or the network gains nothing from a better nice value, and a latency problem caused by a lock held by a low-priority thread is not solved by raising the waiter. Find what the waiting thread is actually waiting for before touching priorities.

questions.prompt: A high-priority control thread misses deadlines. Traces show it blocked on a lock held by a low-priority logger, while a medium-priority analytics thread runs. What is happening?

choices.label: Priority inversion: Medium keeps Low from releasing the lock
Deadlock: High and Low each hold a lock the other needs
Starvation: the scheduler skips High in favour of others
Livelock: High and Low keep yielding to each other

questions.explanation: High waits for Low, and Medium outranks Low, so the lock holder cannot run: a classic inversion. Deadlock needs a cycle of waits, which Medium breaks; High runs when it is runnable but it is blocked, not ignored; and livelock needs threads actively retrying, which none is.

questions.prompt: Which change bounds High’s wait to roughly the length of Low’s critical section?

choices.label: Raising Medium’s priority above High’s for fairness
Giving High a lower nice value than the others
Enabling priority inheritance on the shared mutex
Adding a second core so Medium runs elsewhere

questions.explanation: Inheritance lifts Low to High’s priority while High waits, so Medium cannot preempt it and the lock is released after Low’s section. Raising Medium makes things worse, nice values do not affect real-time priorities or lock waits, and a second core helps only by luck, since Medium and Low can still share one.

questions.prompt: Two CPU-bound threads share one core under the normal policy. One runs at nice 0, the other at nice 10. What happens?

choices.label: The nice 0 thread runs and the other waits until it ends
Both get half the core each, since nice only affects I/O
The nice 10 thread runs first until it has finished
Both run; the nice 0 thread gets a much larger share

questions.explanation: Under the normal policy, nice sets a weight, and each nice step changes it by about 1.25 times, so ten steps give the nice 0 thread roughly nine times the share, but both progress. Strict precedence is how real-time policies behave, nice has nothing to do with I/O, and higher nice means lower priority.

questions.prompt: A real-time thread at priority 50 enters an infinite loop on a 1-core machine. What do you expect?

choices.label: Normal threads still get a small slice of each second
The kernel demotes it to normal priority within a second
It runs only when no normal thread wants the CPU
Other threads stop running until it is killed

questions.explanation: Real-time threads outrank all normal ones, but Linux by default reserves 5% of each second for non-real-time work, so normal threads crawl rather than stop. The kernel does not demote it, real-time threads run ahead of normal ones rather than after, and the throttling margin prevents a total freeze.

questions.prompt: Two CPU-bound threads share one core. Their scheduler weights are 1,024 (nice 0) and 335 (nice 5). Roughly what percentage of the core does the nice 0 thread get?
assumptions: Shares are proportional to weights
Both threads are always runnable
questions.explanation: Sanity check: five nice steps of about 1.25 times each give a ratio of about 3 to 1, so roughly three quarters and one quarter; nice reshapes shares but never stops the weaker thread.

questions.prompt: Order the events of a bounded inversion when the mutex uses priority inheritance.

items.label: Medium wakes but cannot preempt the boosted Low
Low takes the lock
Low releases the lock, drops back to its own priority, and High runs
High blocks on the lock and Low inherits High’s priority

questions.explanation: Boost on block, release, un-boost: High waits only for the rest of Low’s critical section.

flashcards.back: High waits on a lock held by Low, while Medium preempts Low, so High waits on Medium.
A lock holder temporarily runs at the priority of the highest thread waiting for it.
Nice sets proportional shares among normal threads; real-time priorities strictly preempt.

sources.title: Real-Time group scheduling, Linux kernel documentation

mechanism.title: How priorities interact with locks
steps: Each core picks the next thread from its run queue: any runnable real-time thread first, highest priority first, then normal threads by their weighted fair share.
A thread that blocks on a lock leaves the run queue; its priority no longer matters until it is woken. The lock holder keeps its own priority.

If a thread of middle priority becomes runnable, it preempts the low-priority holder, and the high-priority waiter now depends indirectly on the middle thread finishing. The wait is unbounded: as long as middle-priority work exists, the holder cannot run.

With priority inheritance, blocking on the lock records the waiter, and the kernel raises the holder to the waiter’s priority. Chains are followed: if the holder is itself waiting on another lock, that holder is boosted too.
With a priority ceiling, each lock has a fixed priority at least as high as any thread that uses it; a thread holding it runs at that priority, which also prevents some deadlocks.
Real-time scheduling adds throttling: by default real-time threads may use 950 ms of every 1,000 ms, leaving 50 ms for everything else so a runaway thread can still be stopped.

useWhen: Use priority inheritance on locks shared by threads with different real-time priorities.
Use real-time policies only for short, bounded work with hard latency needs, such as audio or control loops.
avoidWhen: Avoid sharing locks between real-time threads and threads that do unbounded work.
Avoid treating nice values as a fix for latency caused by waiting.

rows: Boosts a holder while a higher thread waits
Boosts every holder to the lock’s ceiling
Ceilings must be assigned and kept correct

numbers.title: How long High really waits
assumptions: Low’s critical section takes 1 ms; Medium runs CPU work in 50 ms bursts; High’s deadline is 10 ms (illustrative)
steps: Without inheritance, worst case: High waits for Medium’s burst plus the rest of Low’s section, 50 + 1 = 51 ms.
That misses the 10 ms deadline by 41 ms, and two Medium bursts in a row would double it.
With inheritance: High waits for at most the remainder of Low’s section, about 1 ms.
High then has about 9 ms of its 10 ms budget left for its own work.
numbers.result: Inheritance turns a 51 ms worst case into about 1 ms here; the bound depends only on the critical section, not on unrelated work.

india.title: An inversion on another planet
india.label: Publicly reported
india.body: NASA’s Mars Pathfinder lander, which landed in 1997, suffered repeated system resets on the surface. Engineers publicly described the cause as priority inversion: a low-priority meteorological task held a mutex needed by a high-priority bus management task, while medium-priority communication tasks kept the low one from running, so a watchdog detected the missed deadline and reset the computer. The fix, uploaded from Earth, enabled priority inheritance on that mutex.

pitfalls.trap: “Make the slow thread a higher priority.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d first check what it is waiting for; if it’s a lock held by a lower thread, I’d use priority inheritance.”
“It makes it preempt others, not run faster; unbounded work at real-time priority starves the machine.”

takeaways: A high-priority waiter can be held up by medium-priority work.
Priority inheritance or ceilings bound the wait to one critical section.
Nice sets shares; real-time priorities strictly preempt.
Real-time threads must do short, bounded work.

interactive.title: How long does High wait?
interactive.prompt: On one core, Low (priority 10) takes a lock for a 2 ms update. High (priority 90) then blocks on that lock. Medium (priority 50) wakes and computes for 40 ms. The mutex uses no special protocol.

choices.label: About 42 ms: Medium runs first, then Low finishes
choices.feedback: Right: Medium outranks Low, so the lock holder cannot run until Medium is done.

choices.label: About 2 ms, since High outranks everyone
choices.feedback: High is blocked, not runnable, so its priority does not help Low.

choices.label: Forever: this is a deadlock
choices.feedback: There is no cycle; once Medium finishes, Low releases the lock.

interactive.reveal: Enable priority inheritance on the mutex and Low runs at priority 90 while High waits, so Medium cannot preempt it and High waits about 2 ms.

seeAlso.why: How the scheduler picks among runnable threads
Lock waiting is where inversions happen
Priority ceilings also help prevent some deadlocks

title: Thread Pools: Sizing, Queues and Rejection
objectives: Size a pool from cores and the share of time tasks spend waiting
Bound the queue and choose what happens when it is full
Avoid deadlocks where tasks wait on the pool they run in

cards.title: Why pools exist
cards.body: Creating a thread costs memory for its stack and a trip through the kernel, and thousands of threads compete for a few cores. A pool keeps a fixed set of worker threads that take tasks from a queue. Three numbers define it: how many workers, how long the queue may grow, and what happens to a task that arrives when both are full.

cards.title: Worked example: sizing from wait time
cards.body: A service on 8 cores (illustrative numbers).
steps: Each task computes for 10 ms and waits 40 ms on a database
A worker keeps a core busy only 10 ÷ 50 = 20% of the time
To keep 8 cores busy: 8 × (1 + 40 ÷ 10) = 40 workers
Cross-check with arrivals: at 800 tasks a second each lasting 50 ms, about 800 × 0.05 = 40 tasks are in progress at once
More workers than this cannot add CPU; they only queue on the database

cards.title: Trap: the unbounded queue
cards.body: A pool with an unlimited queue never rejects anything, so overload shows up as tasks waiting longer and longer, memory growing, and clients timing out on work the server will still do later. Bound the queue to what you can finish within the caller’s deadline, and decide the overflow policy: reject quickly with an error, run the task on the submitting thread to slow it down, or drop the oldest work.

cards.title: Misconception: one big pool is simplest
cards.body: If a task running in a pool submits a sub-task to the same pool and waits for it, every worker can end up waiting for sub-tasks that have no free worker to run them: a deadlock. One slow dependency can also occupy every worker and stall unrelated work. Give each kind of blocking work its own bounded pool (bulkheads), and never block a worker on the pool it belongs to.

cards.title: Watching a pool
cards.body: Four measurements show a pool’s health: active workers, queue length, time tasks spend queued, and rejections. Queue time rising while workers are all busy means the pool or its downstream is saturated; workers idle while the queue grows means tasks are stuck waiting on something. Alert on queue time, which is what callers feel, rather than on thread count.

questions.prompt: A CPU-bound image resizer runs on a 16-core machine and never waits on I/O. About how many pool workers should it start with?

choices.label: About 16, one per core
About 160, so that tasks do not queue
About 4, to leave cores free for the kernel
One per pending request, created on demand

questions.explanation: Tasks that never wait can keep at most one core busy each, so about one worker per core uses the machine fully. More workers add switching and cache misses without more CPU, a quarter of the cores wastes capacity, and one thread per request is the unbounded model a pool exists to avoid.

questions.prompt: Under a traffic spike, a service’s latency climbs from 50 ms to 40 s and memory keeps growing, but it returns no errors. What is the most likely design flaw?

choices.label: The pool has too few workers for normal traffic
Tasks queue without limit instead of being rejected
The garbage collector is tuned for throughput
Workers are pinned to specific cores

questions.explanation: Growing latency and memory with no errors is the signature of an unbounded queue absorbing overload. Too few workers would also show at normal load, collector tuning does not explain 40 s waits with steady growth, and pinning affects cache behaviour, not queueing.

questions.prompt: A report task runs in a 10-worker pool, submits 3 sub-tasks to the same pool and waits for them. With 10 reports in flight, everything stops. Why?

choices.label: Sub-tasks are run in reverse order of submission
The pool’s queue is too short to hold 30 sub-tasks
All 10 workers wait on sub-tasks no worker is free to run
Waiting on a future is not allowed inside a pool

questions.explanation: Every worker holds a report that waits on queued sub-tasks, and no worker is free to run them, so nothing progresses. Ordering does not matter, a longer queue still leaves the sub-tasks unrun, and waiting is allowed; it is waiting on your own pool that deadlocks.

questions.prompt: A batch importer submits work to a pool far faster than the pool finishes it. Which overflow policy fits best?
constraints: The importer can slow down without harm

approaches.label: Run overflow on the submitting thread
approaches.description: When the queue is full, the importer executes the task itself, which slows its submissions.

approaches.label: Reject overflow with an error
approaches.description: The pool throws away work it cannot queue and reports a failure.

approaches.label: Use an unbounded queue
approaches.description: Accept everything and let the queue grow.

rationaleOptions.label: It applies backpressure, so the producer slows to the pool’s pace
It keeps memory bounded because the queue never grows past its limit
It guarantees the fastest possible completion of each record
It removes the need to size the pool at all

questions.explanation: Caller-runs turns overflow into backpressure: the importer does the work itself and submits more slowly, nothing is dropped, and the queue stays bounded. Rejecting would lose records unless the importer retried, and an unbounded queue breaks the memory limit. It does not make each record faster, and the pool still needs a size.

questions.prompt: A service runs on 4 cores. Each task computes for 5 ms and then waits 45 ms on remote calls. How many workers keep all 4 cores busy?
assumptions: Waiting uses no CPU
Enough tasks are always queued
questions.explanation: Design implication: the remote service must handle 40 concurrent calls from this one instance; if it cannot, more workers just move the queue downstream.

questions.prompt: Order what a typical pool does as load rises on a newly submitted task.

items.label: Otherwise start an extra worker if below the maximum
Give it to an idle worker if one exists
Otherwise apply the overflow policy
Otherwise place it in the queue if there is room

questions.explanation: Idle worker, then queue, then grow, then reject or push back. Note that with an unbounded queue the last two steps never happen.

flashcards.back: An unbounded queue turns overload into ever-growing latency and memory with no errors.
Tasks wait on sub-tasks queued to the same pool with no free worker to run them.

mechanism.title: How a pool handles a task
steps: A submitted task first goes to an idle worker if there is one, or a new worker is started while the pool is below its core size.
If all core workers are busy, the task waits in the queue. A bounded queue has a capacity; an unbounded one accepts everything.
Some pools start extra workers, up to a maximum, only when the queue is full; with an unbounded queue that never happens, so the maximum has no effect.
When the queue is full and the pool is at its maximum, the overflow policy runs: reject with an error, run on the caller, or discard a task.
Workers loop: take a task, run it, repeat. Extra workers above the core size exit after an idle timeout.
Throughput is capped by the slowest of workers × 1 ÷ task time, available cores, and what downstream services can take; queue time rises sharply as utilisation nears that cap.

useWhen: Use separate bounded pools for work with different dependencies.
Use caller-runs or rejection to push overload back to producers.
avoidWhen: Avoid unbounded queues on request paths.
Avoid blocking a pool’s worker on tasks submitted to the same pool.

numbers.title: Sizing a pool and its queue
assumptions: 1,000 requests a second; each takes 2 ms of CPU and 18 ms waiting on a cache; 8 cores; callers time out at 200 ms (illustrative)
steps: Concurrent requests in progress: 1,000 × 0.020 s = 20.
CPU needed: 1,000 × 2 ms = 2 core-seconds per second, so 8 cores are 25% busy.
Workers: 20 at steady load; allow 40 for bursts, still far below what 8 cores can switch between.
Queue: a task queued behind 40 workers each taking 20 ms waits about 20 ms per batch of 40, so 200 ms allows about 10 batches; cap the queue at about 400 and reject beyond.
numbers.result: Forty workers and a queue of about 400 keep queued tasks inside the 200 ms deadline; anything more would only be answered after the caller has given up.

india.title: What a standard pool’s documentation warns
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The documentation for one widely used standard library thread pool explains that using an unbounded queue causes new tasks to wait when all core threads are busy, so no more than the core number of threads is ever created and the maximum pool size has no effect. It notes that this allows unbounded growth of the queue when tasks arrive faster than they are processed, that the default handler rejects overflow with an error, and that the caller-runs policy provides a simple feedback mechanism that slows the rate at which new tasks are submitted.

pitfalls.trap: “Make the pool bigger until latency drops.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d check whether workers are waiting downstream; if so, more workers only move the queue there.”

pitfalls.trap: “An unbounded queue means we never drop requests.”
pitfalls.say: “It means we answer them after the caller has timed out; I’d bound it and reject early.”

takeaways: Size pools from cores and the wait-to-compute ratio.
Bound the queue to what fits in the caller’s deadline.
Choose an overflow policy deliberately; caller-runs gives backpressure.
Never block a worker on its own pool.

interactive.title: What does doubling the pool do?
interactive.prompt: A pool of 50 workers is saturated; every task spends most of its time waiting on a database that already runs at 100% CPU. Someone doubles the pool to 100.

choices.label: Throughput stays about the same and database latency rises
choices.feedback: Right: the database is the bottleneck, so more concurrent calls only lengthen its queue.

choices.label: Throughput roughly doubles because twice as many tasks run
choices.feedback: Twice as many tasks wait, but the database finishes queries no faster.

choices.label: Throughput falls to zero as the pool deadlocks
choices.feedback: Nothing here waits on its own pool, so there is no deadlock.

interactive.reveal: Pool size only helps while the pool itself is the bottleneck. Find the saturated resource first; here it is the database, so reduce or cache its queries, or limit concurrency to what it can serve.

seeAlso.why: Every extra worker adds context switches
Pool queues are guarded by the locks covered here

title: Page Replacement, Swapping and Thrashing
objectives: Explain how the kernel chooses which pages to evict when memory runs short
Estimate how a small fault rate slows every memory access
Recognise thrashing and tell swap activity from swap usage

cards.title: Two kinds of pages to evict
cards.body: When free memory runs low, the kernel reclaims pages. Clean file pages, such as program code or cached file data, can simply be dropped and read back from the file later. Dirty file pages must be written back first. Anonymous pages, such as heap and stack, have no file behind them, so they can be evicted only if there is swap space to write them to.

cards.title: Approximating least recently used
cards.body: Evicting the page used longest ago would be ideal but tracking exact order on every access is too costly. Hardware sets an accessed bit when a page is touched; the kernel periodically scans and clears these bits, keeping pages seen again on an active list and moving the rest to an inactive list, from which it evicts. This clock-like scheme keeps recently used pages in memory at low cost.

cards.title: Worked example: one fault in ten thousand
cards.body: Average access time when some accesses fault to disk (illustrative).
steps: A memory access takes 100 ns
A fault that reads a page from a hard disk takes 10 ms, which is 10,000,000 ns
With one fault per 10,000 accesses: 100 + 10,000,000 ÷ 10,000 = 1,100 ns
The average access is 11 times slower, from a fault rate of only 0.01%
With a solid-state disk at 100 µs per fault, the same rate costs 100 + 10 = 110 ns

cards.title: Trap: turning off swap does not stop thrashing
cards.body: Without swap, anonymous pages cannot be evicted, so under pressure the kernel evicts what it still can: file pages, including the code of running programs. Programs then fault their own instructions back in from disk over and over, and the machine thrashes anyway, or the out-of-memory killer ends a process. Swap is not the cause of thrashing; a working set larger than memory is.

cards.title: Misconception: swap in use means memory is short
cards.body: Pages swapped out long ago and never touched again can sit in swap indefinitely, freeing memory for useful cache. What matters is the rate of pages moving in and out per second, and how long tasks stall waiting for memory, which Linux reports as memory pressure stall information. High swap usage with near-zero swap-in is fine; steady swap-in under load is the warning sign.

questions.prompt: Memory is short and the machine has no swap. Which pages can the kernel still reclaim?

choices.label: Heap pages of idle processes, which are written to a temporary file
Only pages belonging to the process using the most memory
File-backed pages, such as cached data and program code
None, so it ends a process straight away

questions.explanation: File-backed pages can be dropped and re-read from their files, after writing back any that are dirty. Anonymous heap pages need swap, and the kernel does not invent a temporary file for them. Reclaim spans all processes rather than the largest one, and the out-of-memory killer runs only after reclaim fails.

questions.prompt: A server shows 6 GB of swap in use, swap-in near zero and steady response times. What should you conclude?

choices.label: Memory is short; add RAM before it gets worse
Rarely used pages were swapped out and are staying there
Swap is broken, because used swap should be read back
The page cache has been disabled by the kernel

questions.explanation: Pages that are never touched again stay in swap harmlessly; the low swap-in rate and steady latency show no pressure. Usage alone does not show a shortage, nothing requires swapped pages to return, and the page cache is unaffected.

questions.prompt: Under load, a host’s CPU is mostly idle, disk reads are at maximum, and every request is slow. Memory pressure stall figures are high. What is happening?

choices.label: The working set no longer fits, so pages keep faulting in
The CPU is overheating and throttling its clock speed
The disk is failing and retrying each read several times
Too many threads are spinning on locks in user space

questions.explanation: Idle CPU, saturated reads and high memory stalls together mean processes spend their time waiting for pages that were evicted and are needed again: thrashing. Throttling would show busy CPUs running slowly, a failing disk would not raise memory stall time, and spinning threads would make the CPU busy, not idle.

questions.prompt: A host thrashes after a new service is added. Which fix addresses the cause?

choices.label: Disable swap so that nothing can be paged out
Raise each process’s scheduling priority
Add more swap space on a faster disk
Cut memory use or move a service elsewhere

questions.explanation: Thrashing means the combined working sets exceed RAM, so reduce demand or add memory. Disabling swap shifts eviction to program code and invites the out-of-memory killer, priorities do not make memory larger, and more swap gives more room to page into without reducing the paging.

questions.prompt: A memory access takes 100 ns. One in every 10,000 accesses faults and waits 10 ms for a disk read. What is the average time per access in nanoseconds?
assumptions: Faults are spread evenly across accesses
Non-faulting accesses all take 100 ns
questions.formula: access time + fault cost × fault rate
questions.explanation: Sanity check: a 0.01% fault rate makes memory 11 times slower here, which is why even light paging is so visible; to stay within 10% of normal speed the fault rate must be below one in a million.

questions.prompt: Order what happens to an anonymous page that stops being used on a host under memory pressure, until it is evicted.

items.label: It moves to the inactive list
Its contents are written to swap and its frame is freed
The reclaim scan finds its accessed bit clear
It is still not touched before the next scan

questions.explanation: Pages earn eviction by staying untouched across scans; a touch in between would move it back to the active list.

flashcards.front: Which pages need swap to be evicted?
flashcards.back: Anonymous pages, such as heap and stack; file pages can be dropped and re-read.
Working sets exceed RAM, so pages are evicted and faulted back in constantly.
Usage is harmless by itself; sustained swap-in and memory stalls signal pressure.

sources.title: Concepts overview, Linux memory management (kernel documentation)

mechanism.title: How the kernel reclaims memory
steps: Each zone of memory has watermarks. When free pages fall below the low mark, a background reclaim thread wakes and frees pages until the high mark is reached.
Pages sit on active and inactive lists, separately for file and anonymous memory. Reclaim scans inactive pages; a page whose accessed bit was set gets another chance on the active list.

Clean file pages are dropped, dirty ones are written back first, and anonymous pages are written to swap if it exists. A swappiness setting tilts the balance between reclaiming file pages and swapping anonymous ones.
If background reclaim cannot keep up, an allocating process reclaims directly and stalls; this direct reclaim is where latency appears.
A page evicted and then needed again causes a major fault: the process blocks while the page is read back. When most faults are refaults of recently evicted pages, the system is thrashing.

If reclaim fails, the out-of-memory killer picks a process to end, preferring those using the most memory adjusted by a per-process score. Containers add a second layer: each memory control group has its own limit and reclaims, and kills, within itself before the whole host is short.

useWhen: Use swap as a buffer for cold anonymous pages, so RAM holds hot data and cache.
Use memory pressure stall figures to alert on real contention.
avoidWhen: Avoid running working sets close to or above RAM.
Avoid treating swap usage, rather than swap-in rate, as an alarm.

rows: Low, with tasks waiting on I/O

numbers.title: How much paging a service can afford
assumptions: Memory access 100 ns; each fault reads from a solid-state disk in 100 µs; acceptable slowdown 10% (illustrative)
steps: Allowed extra time per access: 10% of 100 ns = 10 ns.
Fault cost: 100 µs = 100,000 ns.
Maximum fault rate: 10 ÷ 100,000 = one fault per 10,000 accesses.
On a hard disk at 10 ms per fault the limit becomes 10 ÷ 10,000,000, one per million accesses, a hundred times stricter.
numbers.result: Even a fast disk allows only about one fault per 10,000 accesses before memory feels 10% slower, so paging must stay rare for hot data.

india.title: What the kernel documentation says about reclaim
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Linux memory management concepts guide explains that pages backed by files can be freed after writing any changes back, while anonymous pages can be reclaimed only by writing them to a swap area. It describes how, when memory runs low, the kernel frees pages by reclaim, and if the system cannot free enough, the out-of-memory killer chooses a task to end. The kernel’s pressure stall documentation adds that memory pressure figures report the share of time tasks are stalled waiting for memory.

pitfalls.trap: “Swap is full, so we need more RAM.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d check swap-in rate and memory stall time; cold pages in swap are harmless.”
“Thrashing comes from working sets bigger than RAM; without swap the kernel evicts program code instead.”

takeaways: File pages can be dropped; anonymous pages need swap.
A tiny fault rate can multiply average access time.
Watch swap-in rate and stall time, not swap usage.
Fix thrashing by cutting demand or adding memory.

interactive.title: What happens without swap?
interactive.prompt: A host has no swap. Its processes’ heaps grow until free memory is nearly gone, and they keep growing slowly.

choices.label: The kernel evicts program code and cache, then kills a process
choices.feedback: Right: only file pages can go, so programs refault their own code, and finally the out-of-memory killer acts.

choices.label: The heaps stop growing because allocation fails at once
choices.feedback: Most allocations succeed until reclaim runs out of options; failure is not immediate.

choices.label: Nothing changes until memory is completely full, then it slows
choices.feedback: Reclaim starts at the low watermark, well before memory is full.

interactive.reveal: Without swap, heap pages are pinned in RAM, so all reclaim pressure lands on file pages, including executable code. Latency degrades before the out-of-memory killer finally ends a process.

seeAlso.why: Page tables and faults that reclaim relies on
The page cache is the main pool of reclaimable file pages
Huge pages change how memory is mapped and reclaimed

title: The TLB and Huge Pages
objectives: Explain what the translation lookaside buffer caches and why misses are costly
Calculate TLB reach for different page sizes
Decide when huge pages help and when transparent ones hurt

cards.title: A cache for address translations
cards.body: Every memory access needs its virtual address translated to a physical one, which would mean walking several levels of page tables each time. The translation lookaside buffer (TLB) is a small hardware cache of recent translations. A hit costs almost nothing; a miss makes the hardware walk the tables, adding several memory accesses, each of which may miss the data caches too.

cards.title: Worked example: TLB reach
cards.body: How much memory a TLB can cover (illustrative entry count).
steps: Suppose the second-level TLB holds 1,536 entries
With 4 KiB pages, reach = 1,536 × 4 KiB = 6 MiB
A 2 GiB hash table accessed at random misses the TLB on almost every lookup
With 2 MiB pages, reach = 1,536 × 2 MiB = 3 GiB, which covers the whole table
Each 2 MiB page also replaces 512 page table entries, so walks that do happen are shorter

cards.title: Explicit and transparent huge pages
cards.body: Huge pages can be reserved explicitly at boot or at run time and mapped by programs that ask for them; they are never swapped and are guaranteed to exist. Transparent huge pages let the kernel use 2 MiB pages for ordinary memory automatically, either everywhere or only where a program advises it, and a background thread merges small pages into huge ones when it can.

cards.title: Trap: transparent huge pages and latency spikes
cards.body: To create a huge page the kernel needs 2 MiB of contiguous free memory. When memory is fragmented it may stop an allocating thread to compact memory, causing pauses, and a program that touches one byte of a region can be given the whole 2 MiB, bloating memory use. Systems with many small, scattered allocations often run better with transparent huge pages limited to programs that request them.

cards.title: Misconception: huge pages make memory faster
cards.body: Huge pages do not make RAM or the data caches faster; they make translation cheaper. A program whose working set already fits in TLB reach, or that streams memory sequentially, sees little change. The gains come for large working sets accessed at random, such as big hash tables, in-memory databases and virtual machines, where page walks are a measurable share of time.

questions.prompt: What does the TLB store?

choices.label: Recently used data lines copied from main memory
Recent virtual-to-physical address translations
The list of pages waiting to be written to swap
Each thread’s registers saved at a context switch

questions.explanation: The TLB caches translations so most accesses skip the page table walk. Data lines live in the data caches, swap candidates are kernel lists in ordinary memory, and saved registers are kept in kernel memory for each thread.

questions.prompt: Which workload is most likely to speed up noticeably with 2 MiB pages?

choices.label: A tool that reads a 50 GB log file once from start to end
A web handler that touches 200 KB of memory per request
A 20 GiB in-memory index probed at random keys
A program that sleeps on network input most of the time

questions.explanation: Random probes across 20 GiB miss a 4 KiB-page TLB constantly, and larger pages raise reach enough to cut those misses. Sequential reads are dominated by disk and prefetching, a 200 KB footprint already fits in TLB reach, and a mostly sleeping program has no translation bottleneck.

questions.prompt: After transparent huge pages were set to apply everywhere, a cache server shows occasional 100 ms pauses and higher memory use. What is the likely cause?

choices.label: The kernel compacts memory to build huge pages and fills sparse regions
Huge pages are written to swap more often than small pages
The TLB is flushed each time a huge page is created
Huge pages make each cache line 2 MiB long

questions.explanation: Building 2 MiB pages can force compaction stalls when memory is fragmented, and sparsely used regions get whole huge pages, raising memory use. Transparent huge pages are usually split before swapping rather than swapped more, creating one does not flush the whole TLB, and cache line size is fixed by hardware.

questions.prompt: Why does switching between two processes typically cost more in TLB terms than switching between two threads of one process?

choices.label: Threads of one process use physical addresses directly
Processes have different address spaces, so translations differ
Process switches also flush the data caches
The TLB stores entries only for the kernel’s own threads

questions.explanation: Threads share one address space, so their TLB entries stay valid; another process has different translations, so entries must be flushed or tagged by address-space ID, and the new process starts with fewer hits. Threads do use virtual addresses, data caches are not flushed on a normal switch, and the TLB holds user translations too.

questions.prompt: A lookup service makes 20 million random probes a second. 40% of them miss the TLB, and each miss costs about 25 ns of page walking. How many milliseconds of core time per second go to page walks?
assumptions: Miss cost does not overlap with other work
Every probe is a single memory access
questions.formula: probes × miss rate × cost per miss
questions.explanation: Design implication: a fifth of a core goes to translation alone; if huge pages cut the miss rate to 4%, that falls to 20 ms, so measuring the miss rate tells you whether huge pages are worth their risks.

questions.prompt: Order what happens on a load instruction whose translation is not in the TLB, until the data arrives.

items.label: The physical address is used to fetch the data
The hardware walks the page table levels in memory
The TLB lookup misses
The translation is installed in the TLB

questions.explanation: Miss, walk, install, access. A fault is raised only if the walk finds no valid entry, which is the page fault case.

flashcards.back: A small hardware cache of virtual-to-physical translations.
Entries × page size; 1,536 entries cover 6 MiB with 4 KiB pages or 3 GiB with 2 MiB pages.
Compaction stalls and memory bloat from sparsely used 2 MiB regions.

mechanism.title: What a TLB miss costs
steps: A load or store presents a virtual address. The core checks a small first-level TLB, then a larger second-level one, in parallel with starting the cache lookup.
On a miss, a hardware page walker reads the page table levels, four on common 64-bit systems, starting from the root held in a register; upper levels are often in the data caches.
If the final entry is valid, the translation is installed in the TLB and the access proceeds. If it is not, a page fault is raised and the kernel takes over.
With a 2 MiB page, the walk stops one level early and one entry covers 512 times as much memory, so both the miss rate and the cost of each miss fall.

Changing address space, as on a switch between processes, invalidates entries unless they are tagged with an address-space identifier; changing a mapping requires shooting down stale entries on other cores, which costs an interrupt to each.
Transparent huge pages are created at fault time when an aligned 2 MiB region is free, or later by a background thread that collapses small pages; failing that, ordinary 4 KiB pages are used.

useWhen: Use huge pages for large, randomly accessed, long-lived memory such as database buffer pools and virtual machine memory.
Use advise-only transparent mode so programs opt in.
avoidWhen: Avoid enabling transparent huge pages everywhere for sparse, fragmented allocation patterns.
Avoid expecting gains for small or sequential working sets.

numbers.title: Is translation worth fixing?
assumptions: A lookup service misses the TLB on 30% of 50 million probes a second; each miss costs about 30 ns of page walking (illustrative)
steps: Walking time: 15,000,000 × 30 ns = 0.45 s of core time per second.
With huge pages covering the table, suppose misses drop to 3%: 1,500,000 × 30 ns = 0.045 s.
Saving: about 0.4 core-seconds per second, nearly half a core freed.
numbers.result: Here huge pages free almost half a core, worth doing; at a 1% miss rate the same change would save under 0.02 cores and not be worth the risks.

india.title: What the kernel documentation says huge pages buy
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The kernel’s memory concepts guide explains that the TLB is usually a scarce resource, and applications with large memory working sets suffer a performance hit because of TLB misses; mapping 2 MiB or 1 GiB pages significantly reduces pressure on the TLB and improves its hit rate. The transparent huge page guide adds that a huge page reduces page faults by a factor of 512 for the region it covers and makes TLB misses run faster, but warns that the kernel may need to compact memory to find contiguous space.

pitfalls.trap: “Turn on huge pages everywhere for speed.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d measure TLB miss rates first and opt in only large, random-access memory.”
“They could be compaction for transparent huge pages; I’d check kernel stall counters too.”

takeaways: The TLB caches translations; misses walk the page tables.
Reach equals entries times page size.
Huge pages help large random-access working sets.
Transparent huge pages can cause compaction pauses and bloat.

interactive.title: Will huge pages help this job?
interactive.prompt: A batch job scans a 100 GB file sequentially, once, processing each record as it goes. Someone proposes enabling huge pages to speed it up.

choices.label: Little change: sequential scanning has few TLB misses per byte
choices.feedback: Right: each 4 KiB page serves 4,096 consecutive bytes, so translation is a tiny share of the work.

choices.label: A large speedup, because 100 GB is far beyond TLB reach
choices.feedback: Size alone does not matter; the access pattern does, and sequential access misses rarely.

choices.label: It will fail, since huge pages cannot hold file data
choices.feedback: Whether file data can use huge pages depends on the file system, but either way the gain here is small.

interactive.reveal: Huge pages pay off when accesses jump around a large working set. A one-pass sequential scan is limited by disk or memory bandwidth, not by translations.

seeAlso.why: Page tables are what the TLB caches
Data caches and locality, the other half of memory speed
Reclaim and compaction interact with huge pages
